course-schedule.pattern: Cycle detection in a directed graph (Kahn's algorithm or DFS colouring)

approaches.name: Repeatedly take any course whose prerequisites are done
approaches.idea: Simulate a student: keep scanning for a course whose prerequisites are all already taken, take it, and repeat. If at some point no course can be taken but some remain, there is a cycle.
steps: Keep a `taken` flag per course.
Repeat: scan all prerequisite pairs to find an untaken course with no untaken prerequisite; take it.
Stop when all are taken (true) or a full scan finds nothing to take (false).
approaches.why: Up to V rounds, each checking all courses against all E prerequisite pairs.

approaches.name: Kahn's algorithm (BFS on in-degrees)
approaches.idea: Track how many unmet prerequisites each course has (its in-degree). Courses with 0 can be taken; taking one lowers the in-degree of the courses that depend on it. If every course is eventually taken, there is no cycle.
steps: Build the graph `b → a` for each pair `[a, b]` and count in-degrees.
Queue every course with in-degree 0.
Pop a course, count it as taken, and decrement each dependent's in-degree, queuing those that reach 0.
Return whether the number taken equals `numCourses`.
approaches.why: Each course is queued once and each edge relaxed once. Courses on a cycle never reach in-degree 0, so they are never counted.

approaches.name: DFS with three colours
approaches.idea: Colour courses white (unvisited), grey (on the current DFS path) and black (finished). Reaching a grey course again means following edges led back into the current path: a cycle.
steps: Build the graph `b → a`.
DFS from every white course: mark it grey, visit each neighbour; if a neighbour is grey, return "cycle"; after all neighbours, mark it black.
Return false if any DFS finds a cycle, else true.
approaches.why: Each course is finished once and each edge explored once. Black courses are never re-explored. The recursion can be V deep.

course-schedule-ii.pattern: Topological sort (Kahn's BFS, or reversed DFS post-order)

approaches.name: Kahn's algorithm: output courses as they become free
approaches.idea: Take courses with no remaining prerequisites first. The order in which Kahn's algorithm removes courses is a valid order; if not all courses get removed, there is a cycle.
steps: Build `b → a` edges and in-degrees.
Queue every course with in-degree 0.
Pop a course, append it to the order, and decrement its dependents' in-degrees, queuing those that reach 0.
Return the order if it has all courses, else an empty array.
approaches.why: Each course and edge is handled once; the graph and queue take O(V + E).

approaches.name: DFS post-order, reversed
approaches.idea: In a DFS, a course finishes only after every course that depends on it has finished. So the finishing order lists dependents first; reversing it gives a valid schedule. A grey (in-progress) course met again means a cycle.
steps: Build `b → a` edges; colour all courses white.
DFS from each white course: grey on entry; on meeting grey, report a cycle; after the neighbours, mark black and append the course to `post`.
If there was a cycle, return an empty array; otherwise return `post` reversed.
approaches.why: Each course and edge is processed once; the recursion can be V deep.

course-schedule-iv.pattern: Transitive closure (reachability for all pairs) in a DAG

approaches.name: A fresh search for every query
approaches.idea: `u` is a prerequisite of `v` exactly when `v` is reachable from `u` along the edges `a → b`. Answer each query with its own BFS.
steps: Build the graph `a → b` for every pair `[a, b]`.
For each query `[u, v]`, BFS from `u` and answer whether `v` is reached.
approaches.why: Each of the Q queries (up to 10⁴) may explore the whole graph.

approaches.name: Precompute all reachability with Floyd–Warshall
approaches.idea: With at most 100 courses, compute `reach[i][j]` for every pair once. `i` reaches `j` if it does directly, or via some middle course `k` that `i` reaches and that reaches `j`. Then every query is a table lookup.
steps: Set `reach[a][b] = true` for every prerequisite pair.
For each middle course `k`, for each `i`, for each `j`: `reach[i][j] |= reach[i][k] && reach[k][j]`.
Answer each query `[u, v]` with `reach[u][v]`.
approaches.why: V³ = 10⁶ steps once, then O(1) per query. Considering middle courses in the outer loop is what makes the triple loop correct.

minimum-height-trees.pattern: Peel leaves layer by layer (topological trimming) to find the tree's centre

approaches.name: BFS height from every node
approaches.idea: Root the tree at each node in turn, measure the height with a BFS, and keep the nodes with the smallest height.
steps: Build the adjacency lists.
For each node, BFS to find the number of levels below it (its height).
Return all nodes whose height equals the minimum.
approaches.why: n BFS runs of O(n) each; for n = 2·10⁴ that is 4·10⁸ steps.

approaches.name: Trim leaves until one or two nodes remain
approaches.idea: The best roots are the centre of the tree's longest path. Removing all current leaves shortens every longest path by 2 from both ends, so repeatedly peeling leaves leaves the centre: one node, or two adjacent nodes.
steps: If `n <= 2`, return all nodes.
Compute degrees; queue every leaf (degree 1). Let `remaining = n`.
While `remaining > 2`: remove the whole current layer of leaves (`remaining −= layer size`); each removal lowers its neighbour's degree, and neighbours that become leaves form the next layer.
Return the nodes still in the queue.
approaches.why: Each node is removed once and each edge looked at twice — the same idea as Kahn's algorithm, applied from the outside in.

find-eventual-safe-states.pattern: Nodes that cannot reach a cycle: DFS colouring, or Kahn's algorithm on the reversed graph

approaches.name: From every node, search for a reachable cycle
approaches.idea: A node is unsafe exactly when some path from it reaches a cycle. For each node, run a fresh DFS with grey/black colours and see whether it finds a back edge.
steps: For each node `s`: reset the colours and DFS from `s`.
If the DFS ever reaches a grey node, `s` can reach a cycle: it is unsafe.
Collect the nodes for which no cycle was found (in increasing order).
approaches.why: Each of the V searches can explore the whole graph; nothing is reused between them.

approaches.name: One DFS with colours shared by all nodes
approaches.idea: Run the colour DFS once over the whole graph and keep the colours. A node that finishes (black) cannot reach a cycle, so it is safe; a node left grey when a cycle is found stays grey and is unsafe — and anything that later reaches it is unsafe too.
steps: Colours: 0 unvisited, 1 visiting (or unsafe), 2 safe.
`safe(u)`: if coloured, return `color[u] == 2`. Otherwise set 1; if any neighbour is not safe, return false (leaving `u` at 1).
If all neighbours are safe, set `color[u] = 2` and return true.
Return every `u` with `safe(u)` true, in order.
approaches.why: Each node is fully processed once and each edge followed once, because results are remembered in the colours.

approaches.name: Kahn's algorithm on the reversed graph
approaches.idea: Terminal nodes are safe. A node becomes safe once all of its outgoing edges lead to safe nodes. Reverse every edge and count each node's remaining unsafe outgoing edges; peeling from the terminals works exactly like Kahn's algorithm.
steps: For each edge `u → v`, record `u` in `reverse[v]`; `out[u]` = number of outgoing edges of `u`.
Queue every node with `out == 0` (terminal).
Pop `v`, mark it safe; for each `u` in `reverse[v]`, decrease `out[u]` and queue `u` when it reaches 0.
Return the safe nodes in increasing order.
approaches.why: Each node and edge is processed once; no recursion, so very deep graphs are no problem.

approaches.name: Repeatedly make any recipe whose ingredients are all available
approaches.idea: Keep a set of what you have. Scan the recipes again and again; whenever all of a recipe's ingredients are available, make it and add it to the set. Stop when a full scan makes nothing new.
steps: Put the supplies in a set `have`.
Repeat: for each recipe not made yet, if all its ingredients are in `have`, add it to `have` and to the answer.
Stop after a pass that makes no new recipe.
approaches.why: Up to R passes (one new recipe per pass in the worst case), each checking every recipe's I ingredients.

approaches.name: Kahn's algorithm: supplies unlock recipes
approaches.idea: Each recipe waits on a count of missing ingredients (its in-degree). Start a queue with the supplies; each item taken from the queue satisfies one need of every recipe that uses it. A recipe whose count reaches 0 can be made, and becomes an item itself.
steps: For each recipe `i`, set `need[i] = ingredients[i].length`, and add `i` to `usedBy[ingredient]` for each ingredient.
Queue all supplies.
Pop an item; for each recipe in `usedBy[item]`, decrease its `need`; at 0, add the recipe to the answer and queue its name.
Return the answer. Recipes in a cycle, or needing something unavailable, never reach 0.
approaches.why: Every supply and recipe is queued at most once, and every ingredient link is followed once.

sort-items-by-groups-respecting-dependen.pattern: Two-level topological sort: order the groups, then the items inside each group

approaches.name: Topologically sort groups and items separately, then combine
approaches.idea: Give every ungrouped item its own new group, so every item belongs to exactly one group. A dependency between items in different groups becomes an edge between their groups; one inside a group stays an item edge. Sort the groups topologically, sort the items topologically, then output each group's items (in item order) in group order.
steps: Assign group ids `m, m + 1, …` to items with group −1.
For each `before → i`: add item edge `before → i`; if their groups differ, add group edge `group[before] → group[i]`.
Topologically sort items and groups with Kahn's algorithm; if either has a cycle, return `[]`.
Bucket the sorted items by group, then concatenate the buckets in the sorted group order.
approaches.why: Two Kahn passes over at most n items/groups and E dependency edges, plus linear bucketing. Sorting items globally first keeps each group's items in a valid internal order.
